blocks.text: A propeller shaft snaps and the two halves are laid on a bench. One half-face is smooth with curved ripples running out from one edge, the rest is rough and torn. Without any witness, an investigator can read from that surface where the crack started, how long it ran and whether the final break was sudden. The surface is a record.

blocks.markdown: Fractography is the study of fracture surfaces, from the naked eye to the scanning electron microscope. Every failure mechanism leaves its own signature, and the features are read from large to small: macroscopic marks (visible to the eye or a hand lens) first, then microscopic features (SEM). The rule is to **preserve the surface**: do not fit the halves together, clean aggressively or touch the fracture faces.

rows: Smooth, flat region with beach marks; origin at a surface feature; small rough final-fracture zone
Cup-and-cone (tension), necking, shear lips, dull fibrous surface
Flat, bright, granular; no necking; chevron (V) marks pointing to origin
blocks.caption: Typical signatures of the main failure modes.

blocks.title: Beach marks and striations
blocks.text: **Beach marks** (clamshell marks) are macroscopic concentric arcs on a fatigue surface, centred on the origin. Each marks a position of the crack front where loading changed or paused, such as start-up and shutdown. **Striations** are microscopic ripples, each formed by one load cycle; the spacing between neighbouring striations equals the crack advance per cycle, $\mathrm{d}a/\mathrm{d}N$.

blocks.markdown: **Fatigue.** A fatigue crack begins at a stress concentrator (a notch, keyway corner, scratch, weld toe, inclusion) and spreads slowly across a plane normal to the maximum principal stress. Slow growth leaves a smooth, often polished-looking surface. Beach marks show the successive positions of the crack front; they are convex away from the origin. When the remaining section can no longer carry the load, the part fails suddenly, leaving a rough final-fracture zone.

blocks.title: Reading the growth rate from striations
blocks.prompt: Striations on a fatigue surface are $0.2\ \mu\text{m}$ apart at a certain crack length. If the material obeys $\mathrm{d}a/\mathrm{d}N=C\Delta K^{m}$ with $C=10^{-11}$ and $m=3$ (m/cycle, MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$; typical steel constants), estimate the local $\Delta K$.
blocks.answer: About 27.1 MPa sqrt(m). Closer to the origin the striations would be finer, since $\Delta K$ is lower there.

blocks.markdown: **Ductile and brittle overload.** In a ductile tensile overload, the specimen necks, microvoids nucleate and join (microvoid coalescence) and leave a dull fibrous surface covered in dimples. The classic macroscopic form is **cup-and-cone**: a flat, fibrous central zone formed by void linkage where the triaxial stress is high, surrounded by a 45-degree shear lip. A brittle (cleavage) fracture instead splits atomic planes across grains, producing flat, bright, granular facets with little or no contraction and chevron marks that point back to the origin.

**Locating the initiation site.** Search for the point from which the features diverge. Beach marks are concentric arcs centred on the origin. Radial lines or ratchet marks (steps between multiple origins) fan out from it. In brittle fracture, chevron marks form Vs whose points aim back at the origin. The size of the final-fracture zone relative to the whole section is a rough indicator of the stress level: a large final zone means the stress was high, a small one that the stress was low and the life was long.

blocks.title: Stress at final fracture from the fatigue zone size
blocks.prompt: On a flat steel strap, the smooth fatigue region extends 12 mm from the edge at the origin before the final rough zone begins. Treat it as a single edge crack ($Y=1.12$) in a wide plate with typical toughness $K_{Ic}=50$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. Estimate the peak stress at the instant of final fracture.

steps.text: At the moment of final fracture the crack depth is the fatigue zone depth, $a = 0.012$ m, and $K=K_{Ic}$.
Direction check: a deeper fatigue zone at fracture means a lower peak stress.

items: Smooth region plus beach marks: fatigue. The origin is where the arcs converge.
Dimples and necking: ductile overload. Flat bright facets with chevrons: brittle cleavage.
Small final-fracture zone: low nominal stress, long life. Large final zone: high stress.

blocks.title: Fractography needs context
blocks.text: The surface alone does not state the root cause. Combine it with the loading history, the material properties and the location of the origin. Corrosion, wear or post-fracture rubbing can destroy fine features, so photograph and document the surface before cleaning.

points: Beach marks are macroscopic and striations microscopic evidence of fatigue; striation spacing is the crack growth per cycle.
Ductile fracture shows necking, cup-and-cone and dimples; brittle cleavage shows flat bright facets and chevrons pointing to the origin.
The origin is where beach marks and radial lines converge; the final-fracture zone size indicates stress level.

questions.stem: A fracture surface shows concentric curved arcs centred on a point at the edge, followed by a small rough final zone. What does this indicate?

options.text: A ductile cup-and-cone tensile overload
Fatigue crack growth from an origin at the arc centre
A brittle cleavage fracture
Creep rupture only

questions.correctOptionText: Fatigue crack growth from an origin at the arc centre

distractorRationale.a: Cup-and-cone shows a fibrous cup, not arcs.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: beach marks mark successive crack fronts of fatigue.

questions.explanation: Beach marks are macroscopic arcs centred on the origin and are a hallmark of fatigue. The rough final zone shows where the remaining section failed in overload.

questions.stem: Which fracture surface is characteristic of a ductile tensile overload of a round bar?

options.text: A flat bright surface with chevron marks
Concentric beach marks around an edge origin
A smooth intergranular surface with no deformation
Cup-and-cone with a dull fibrous centre and shear lip, covered in dimples

questions.correctOptionText: Cup-and-cone with a dull fibrous centre and shear lip, covered in dimples
questions.explanation: Necking and microvoid coalescence leave a cup-and-cone profile, with a fibrous central zone, a 45-degree shear lip and dimples at the microscopic level. A flat bright surface would instead point to cleavage.

questions.stem: On a fatigue surface, what does the distance between two adjacent striations represent?

options.text: The crack advance in one load cycle
The crack advance in one hour of service
The grain size
The thickness of the specimen

questions.correctOptionText: The crack advance in one load cycle

distractorRationale.c: Grain size is a separate microstructural feature.

questions.explanation: Each striation forms in one load cycle, so spacing equals $\mathrm{d}a/\mathrm{d}N$ locally. Spacing increases as the crack grows because $\Delta K$ rises.

questions.stem: In a brittle fracture of a steel plate, V-shaped chevron marks are seen on the surface. How are they used to locate the origin?

options.text: The open ends of the V point toward the origin
They always lie on the shear lip
The points of the V point back toward the origin
They are drawn at the final fracture zone only

questions.correctOptionText: The points of the V point back toward the origin

distractorRationale.b: Shear lips are not where chevrons are used.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: chevron points aim at the origin.
distractorRationale.d: They run across the full surface.

questions.explanation: Chevrons are produced as the crack front advances and fan out from the origin, so following the pointed ends of the V leads back to the starting site. The open ends of the Vs point in the direction of crack travel.

questions.stem: A fracture surface is flat, bright and granular, with no necking and no beach marks. Which is the most likely mode?

options.text: Brittle cleavage fracture
Ductile cup-and-cone fracture
Slow fatigue crack growth
Creep rupture with large strain

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cleavage facets reflect light and show little deformation.

questions.explanation: Cleavage cleaves atomic planes with very little plastic deformation. This leaves flat, bright facets, whereas ductile fracture leaves a dull fibrous surface and fatigue leaves beach marks.

questions.stem: Striations on a fatigue surface are $0.8\ \mu\text{m}$ apart over a region 0.40 mm long in the direction of crack growth. Assuming one striation per cycle and constant spacing, how many cycles did it take to grow across that region?
questions.explanation: Number of cycles equals distance divided by spacing: $0.40\times10^{-3}/0.8\times10^{-6}=500$ cycles. The spacing and the distance must be expressed in the same unit.

questions.stem: A steel has $\mathrm{d}a/\mathrm{d}N=C\Delta K^3$ with $C=2\times10^{-11}$ (m/cycle, MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$). Striations are $1.0\ \mu\text{m}$ apart. Estimate the local stress intensity range $\Delta K$ in MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$.
questions.explanation: $\Delta K=(\mathrm{d}a/\mathrm{d}N/C)^{1/3}=(10^{-6}/(2\times10^{-11}))^{1/3}=(5\times10^{4})^{1/3}=36.8$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. The result is a plausible value for stable growth.

questions.stem: A flat bar fractured with a smooth fatigue region 8 mm deep (single edge crack, $Y=1.12$) before the final rough zone. Taking $K_{Ic}=45$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ (assumed), estimate the peak stress at final fracture in MPa.
questions.explanation: At final fracture $K=K_{Ic}$ with $a=0.008$ m, so $\sigma=K_{Ic}/(Y\sqrt{\pi a})=45/(1.12\times0.1585)=253.4$ MPa. A deeper fatigue zone would imply a lower stress.

questions.stem: Contrast ductile and brittle fracture surfaces in terms of macroscopic appearance, microscopic features and the underlying mechanism.
markingGuide: Ductile: necking, cup-and-cone, dull fibrous surface, shear lips
Ductile microscopic features: dimples from microvoid nucleation, growth and coalescence; high energy
Brittle: flat, bright, granular surface, no contraction, chevron marks
Brittle microscopic features: cleavage facets and river patterns; splitting of atomic planes with low energy
Notes the role of temperature, strain rate and constraint in selecting the mode
questions.explanation: Ductile fracture needs extensive plastic flow and leaves dimpled fibrous surfaces. Brittle cleavage occurs with little plasticity and leaves flat bright facets, particularly at low temperature or high constraint.

questions.stem: A rotating steel shaft fails. The fracture face shows a smooth region with concentric beach marks centred on the corner of a keyway, with several small steps (ratchet marks) at the shaft surface near that corner, and a small, rough final-fracture region on the opposite side. (a) Identify the failure mode and the initiation site. (b) What do the ratchet marks and the size of the final zone tell you about the loading? (c) Propose one design change.
markingGuide: Fatigue failure, from beach marks and smooth surface
Origin is at the keyway corner where the arcs converge, a stress concentration
Multiple ratchet marks show several initiation sites, indicating a high stress concentration
Small final zone indicates a low nominal stress and a long life
Design change, for example a keyway with a generous fillet radius, shot peening, or a spline or interference fit to reduce the stress concentration
questions.explanation: The converging arcs identify a fatigue crack that began at the keyway corner, and the multiple ratchet marks indicate several origins in a severe stress concentration. The small final zone shows the nominal stress was low, so a larger fillet radius or another change that lowers the local stress is the best remedy.
